content: 1. Health services management and support for other pillars of a Health Promoting School (HPS), such as health-related school policies, school ethos, safe learning environments, and skills-based health education, should be delivered or supervised by a full-time or part-time health worker. 2. Within the context of School Health Services (SHS), a health worker is defined as a health or allied professional who provides dedicated services to school-going learners. These services are not available to other population groups, regardless of the site where the services are provided. 3. Comparators in studies could include SHS versus no SHS, different types of SHS, or similar programs delivered through community-based general or child/adolescent clinics. If services were delivered only by trained teachers without supervision by a health worker, they were excluded from the analysis. 4. Critical effectiveness outcomes were defined as improvements in outcomes related to short-term mortality or morbidity that would otherwise require acute major health service expenditure or improvements in key educational metrics. Examples include suicide-related outcomes (ideation, plans, gestures, attempts), hospitalizations, emergency department visits, school absences, and academic performance (e.g., grade-point average). 5. Important effectiveness outcomes were defined as those affecting chronic morbidity, the academic climate, or SHS coverage. Examples include violence, sexual health, physical activity, health complaints, quality of life, mental health, substance use (tobacco, alcohol, or drug use), academic expectations, school engagement, and coverage. 6. Critical economic effectiveness outcomes included cost savings, cost-benefit ratios, and cost-effectiveness ratios. 7. A systematic review of the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive SHS screened 8,966 records for potential eligibility, with 443 full-text articles assessed. Eighteen high-quality studies, all using controlled designs, were included. These studies were primarily from high-income countries (HICs), but 19 supplementary observational studies from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) were also included. 8. Data were extracted from all eligible studies, and quality assessments were conducted. For non-randomized controlled studies and cross-sectional studies, the Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool was used. Economic studies were assessed using the Critical Skills Appraisal Programme checklist for economic evaluations. 9. Findings from included studies were synthesized narratively and organized according to outcomes of interest. Where data allowed and studies were methodologically similar, fixed-effects meta-analyses were conducted to estimate effects, including odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for dichotomous data and mean differences with standard deviations for continuous data. 10. Critical acceptability outcomes included user satisfaction as reported by children or adolescents. Important acceptability outcomes included access (e.g., having a regular health-care provider), confidentiality, communication, safety and respect, time spent with the student by the health-care worker, provider satisfaction, and feasibility of implementation from the provider's perspective. 11. Certainty in the findings of studies for each outcome was assessed using GRADE guidance, which evaluates risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias. Controlled evaluation studies started with high certainty and were downgraded based on specific criteria, such as low response rates or small sample sizes. 12. Observational studies started with low certainty but could be upgraded for factors strengthening the evidence base, such as consistency across large numbers of studies and participants, dose-response relationships, or effects present despite confounders. 13. The 2014 WHO handbook for guideline development was used to select an overall certainty rating across outcomes. Strong WHO recommendations are generally based on moderate-to-high certainty evidence, though strong recommendations based on low certainty evidence require special justification. 14. To assess the content of comprehensive SHS in different contexts, an extensive review of global WHO health service procedures and activities for 5–19-year-olds was conducted. This included reviewing 342 recent global WHO publications, of which 149 were used to produce a master list of 531 health service programmatic activities (PAs) relevant to this age group. 15. A global survey of experts was conducted to prioritize interventions for SHS. In July–August 2019, 442 experts from 81 nationalities participated in the survey, ranking 86 interventions as essential, highly suitable, suitable, or unsuitable for SHS. Respondents also suggested additional essential interventions. 16. The survey results showed that most interventions were ranked as suitable to essential within SHS. Health promotion and education interventions were highly ranked as essential, while clinical interventions in areas such as immunization, mass drug administration, screening, and general care were also prioritized. 17. At an October 2019 meeting, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) reviewed survey findings and prioritized interventions for SHS. They categorized 94 interventions as essential, suitable, or unsuitable for inclusion in SHS, based on expert survey results, global WHO health service reviews, and their own expertise. 18. The final list included 71 interventions categorized as essential in SHS everywhere, nine as suitable in SHS everywhere, seven as essential or suitable in certain geographical contexts, and seven as unsuitable in SHS everywhere.
